title: Abhisara: The Tryst
tagline: Rabindranath Tagore's poem of waiting, a delayed meeting and the uneasy question of whether anything was truly understood between the two people involved.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Literature (Paper 2) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). 'Abhisara: The Tryst' by Rabindranath Tagore is named only because it is listed among the prescribed poems in the ISC Class XI prescribed texts. BoardPrep does not reproduce the text of the poem or any CISCE examination question; the explanations and practice questions here are original and are meant to support study of the prescribed poem, not to replace reading it.

overview.intro: 'Abhisara: The Tryst' is one of the five prescribed poems for ISC Class XI English Literature in RHAPSODY: A Collection of ISC Poems. The poem turns on a meeting that is postponed, interrupted or never fully realised, and on the feeling that follows when a promised encounter fails to resolve the relationship between the people involved. The title itself suggests a meeting that is expected, but the poem is often more interested in what waits outside the meeting than in the meeting itself.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Waiting and absence; the meaning of a meeting; communication and uncertainty; silence and expectation; the emotional space between two people

learningOutcomes: Identify the mood of waiting and expectation in the poem.
Discuss how the poem treats a meeting that may not happen as expected.
Explain how silence and distance can be as important as speech.
Describe the emotional relationship between the two figures.
Support observations with brief reference to the poem.

blocks.text: A tryst is a meeting arranged in advance, a moment that carries meaning because it has been waited for. In the poem, that expectation creates tension even before anything happens. The reader is led to think not only about whether the meeting will take place, but about what has been built around it in the meantime. The waiting becomes part of the poem's subject, because expectation itself changes how people feel about one another.

items: The tryst gives the poem its central expectation.
Waiting is not empty; it shapes the mood of the poem.
A meeting may matter because of what is hoped for, not only because of what is said.
The poem works through uncertainty as much as through action.

items.text: A reader might think the poem is only about a missed appointment. A fuller reading notices that the real subject may be the feeling of being suspended between hope and disappointment.
items.note: Expectation can be as emotionally powerful as the event itself.

blocks.text: The poem often suggests that people may be close and yet not fully understand each other. A meeting may occur without clearing up the emotional distance between the characters, or the waiting may expose uncertainty that speech does not resolve. This is one reason the poem remains suggestive rather than simple: it leaves room for what is not said or not completed, and that unfinished quality is part of its meaning.

items: Silence can be as important as what is spoken.
The poem may show two people who are near but not fully connected.
Uncertainty can be part of the poem's emotional power.
The reader is invited to interpret what remains unresolved.

items.text: A student might ask whether the poem is about love, duty, disappointment or all of these. A careful answer notices that the poem does not have to choose one alone; the meeting can stand for several kinds of longing at once.
items.note: The poem's strength lies in its suggestiveness, not in a single simple answer.

blocks.text: The mood of the poem is shaped by patience, anticipation and a certain tenderness mixed with unease. It is not harsh or comic; it is reflective, and it can feel as fragile as the meeting it describes. The tone matters because it affects the reader's response. A poem about a tryst can easily become a plain account of a meeting; this one is more likely to invite the reader into the feeling of waiting.

items: The mood is reflective and expectant.
The tone often suggests tenderness, patience and uncertainty.
The poem's feeling is part of its meaning.
A reader should notice how the mood supports the subject.

items.text: If the poem is read only for its 'story', the emotional quality may be missed. A better reading notices the atmosphere of waiting and the way that atmosphere influences the meaning of the meeting.
items.note: Mood is not decoration; it is one of the poem's main effects.

keyPoints: The poem is built around a meeting that is anticipated and possibly delayed.
Waiting is part of the poem's subject, not just a pause before action.
Silence and uncertainty can be as important as speech.
The mood is reflective and expectant rather than dramatic or comic.
The poem leaves room for interpretation rather than giving one fixed meaning.
Brief reference to the poem supports an answer more effectively than general statements about meeting or love.
examFocus: If the question asks about the tryst, explain what the meeting means in the poem, not just whether it occurs.
When discussing mood, link it to the subject of waiting and uncertainty.
A good answer notices what is left unresolved, not only what is stated.

options: An arranged meeting, often with emotional significance
questions.answer: An arranged meeting, often with emotional significance
questions.explanation: The title points to a meeting that is expected and awaited.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the word as meaning only any casual meeting.

questions.prompt: The poem's central feeling is most likely to be:
options: Waiting and uncertainty about a meeting
questions.answer: Waiting and uncertainty about a meeting
questions.explanation: The poem's interest lies in expectation and the space around the meeting.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the poem as a dramatic narrative with quick action.

questions.prompt: Why can waiting be as important as the meeting itself in this poem?
questions.answer: Because the time of waiting shapes the mood and the relationship, so the poem can be about the feeling of expectation as much as about the meeting that may or may not complete it.
questions.explanation: Waiting creates emotional tension and meaning on its own.
questions.commonMistake: Treating waiting as only an unimportant delay.

questions.prompt: What does silence suggest in a poem like this?
questions.answer: It can suggest what is not said, what is left unresolved, or the distance between two people even when they are close, so silence becomes part of the poem's meaning.
questions.explanation: Silence is often significant in poetry because it can carry emotion or uncertainty.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking silence means nothing is happening in the poem.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the poem presents the relationship between expectation and disappointment.
questions.answer: The poem uses a tryst to set up an expectation, and that expectation makes the waiting meaningful. If the meeting is delayed, uncertain or not fully realised, the poem can show how hope can be disappointed without becoming simple bitterness. The relationship between expectation and disappointment is important because it gives the poem its emotional depth: the waiting is shaped by what the characters want, and the uncertainty leaves room for both tenderness and unease.
questions.explanation: A good answer connects the meeting, waiting and feeling rather than treating the poem as only a story of success or failure.
questions.commonMistake: Reducing the poem to either pure hope or pure disappointment without noticing the complication.
